title: Franchise: The Toy Aisle Outgrosses the Multiplex
dek: On Wikipedia's ledger of 140 media franchises, merchandise, licensing and retail are more than half of lifetime consumer spending. Box office is the part with the red carpet.

blocks.title: DRAFT. Not for publication.

blocks.text: A ledger, not a balance sheet

The list is a volunteer-built estimate of what audiences have spent on a franchise over its whole life, stitched together from press and trade reports. It is not profit. It is not a company valuation. It is not the cash that reached the rights holder.

Wikipedia itself marks the page as needing an update for accuracy, with a tag dated January 2026. [VERIFY: confirm the tag is still on the page, and say so plainly in the published piece.]
One pocket monster versus a galaxy and a cinematic universe

Star Wars started as a 1977 film. The Marvel Cinematic Universe started in 2008. Pokémon started in 1996. Put the first two together and they are still $46.5 billion short of the third.

That is arithmetic on a list, not a verdict on storytelling. It does say where the money on this list tends to live.

blocks.text:
Artometrics splits the ledger into three streams. Merchandise, licensing and retail lead by a wide margin. Video games and box office are close enough that Artometrics' own resampling ranges overlap, so neither can be called the runner-up.

One loose end for the desk: $812.4 billion, $268.2 billion and $265.3 billion, plus the $27.2 billion Artometrics says has no itemised breakdown, add up to $1,373.1 billion. That is about $87.0 billion short of the $1,460.1 billion headline. [VERIFY: find where the remaining ~6% sits, or rewrite the sentence so the shares add up.]
The multiplex is still crowded with sequels

On Artometrics' coding of the 2025 worldwide top ten, nine of the ten biggest films were franchise installments; F1 is the one that is not. That count rests on Box Office Mojo and The Numbers.

The dollars are shakier than the count. For Ne Zha 2, Artometrics reports $2.318 billion on Wikipedia, $2.271 billion on Box Office Mojo and $2.004 billion on The Numbers, and does not average them. [VERIFY: grosses move daily. Re-read all three trackers on the day this publishes.]

blocks.title: What this does not show
blocks.text: A ledger that puts a movie ticket and a plush bear on the same line cannot tell you which one made the other happen. Rows can overlap, rights are sometimes shared, and a lifetime total says nothing about whether the latest release made money.
